Travis Kelce’s $5.35 million Ohio mansion offers the privacy and luxury expected of an NFL star, but making the estate more secluded has proved complicated. The Kansas City Chiefs tight end now faces questions from local residents about landscaping, aging sewer lines and the impact of new barriers on the neighborhood. What began as an effort to improve the property has turned into a wider discussion about balancing personal space with community concerns. With another review scheduled for November, Kelce’s plans for his historic lakeside home remain partly unresolved, despite progress on one major renovation proposal.Travis Kelce purchased the 3.5-acre Bratenahl estate on March 2, 2026, for $5.35 million. Located along Lake Erie near Cleveland, the property stands out for its scale, history and impressive facilities.Known as Moyenage, the mansion dates back to 1904. The historic residence spans 21,140 square feet and features eight bedrooms, 11 bathrooms, seven fireplaces, a sauna, a fitness centre and a heated outdoor pool. Its grounds also include a five-car garage and a guest cottage created from a former gatehouse.However, improving security around such a large property comes with challenges. Kelce’s proposed fencing initially included an eight-foot barrier, prompting concerns from nearby homeowners about lake views and the appearance of the neighborhood.The revised design received unanimous approval from Bratenahl’s Architectural Review Board on September 8. The plan calls for a six-foot black aluminium fence covering approximately 1,190 linear feet, with matching gates and a design intended to complement existing stone walls.Contractor Jacob Kutz explained that the changes addressed residents’ objections, including concerns about preserving views of Lake Erie. The fence will also sit about two feet inside the property boundary to avoid interfering with shared sewer infrastructure.Although the fence has received approval, the mansion’s landscaping plans have encountered further delays. During an October 6 meeting, village officials examined a proposal to plant evergreen trees behind the property.Residents raised concerns about the trees’ eventual height and their possible impact on neighboring homes. Officials indicated that plants growing below 10 feet could offer privacy without creating the same problems. The board approved the front-yard landscaping but postponed its decision on the rear section.Shared utilities have also become a point of contention. Neighbor Katherine Bolton warned that roots from roughly 50 proposed evergreens could damage an aging sewer line reportedly shared with the estate. She said protecting her section of the pipe could cost $75,000.Kelce’s representatives have discussed a $7,500 repair to part of the shared sewer, and the fence design includes access gates for maintenance crews.Bratenahl’s Architectural Review Board plans to reconsider the landscaping proposal on November 10, 2026. Until then, Kelce’s efforts to improve privacy at Moyenage remain subject to local review and the concerns of those living nearby.
Article Summary: Travis Kelce purchased the 3.5-acre Bratenahl estate on March 2, 2026, for $5.35 million. Known as Moyenage, the mansion dates back to 1904. The historic residence spans 21,140 square feet and features eight bedrooms, 11 bathrooms, seven fireplaces, a sauna, a fitness centre and a heated outdoor pool.

Article Title: Andre Agassi and Steffi Graf lost $3 million on $23 million Tiburon mansion after four years of searching for a buyer
Article Text:
Steffi Graf-Andre Agassi (Getty Images)

Andre Agassi's Tiburon estate took years to sell

Why the luxury home struggled to attract buyers

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In 2006, tennis legends Andre Agassi and Steffi Graf made a costly decision involving one of their most impressive real estate assets. After nearly four years on the market, the couple finally found a buyer for their sprawling Tiburon estate in California. The property attracted attention for its breathtaking views, luxury features and celebrity connections. Yet the final sale price came in below what Agassi had paid five years earlier. The deal showed that even a high-end property in a sought-after location can struggle to find the right buyer when its upkeep and price become difficult to justify.Andre Agassi and Steffi Graf agreed to sell the 3.5-acre estate for $20 million, around $3 million less than the $23 million Agassi reportedly paid in 2001. The sale was expected to close in the first week of January 2007, according to Bill Bullock, whose firm represented the couple.The property offered plenty of space and privacy. It featured a 10,500-square-foot main house, separate staff quarters measuring 2,500 square feet, two swimming pools, a stream and a tennis court. Its elevated setting also provided views of the Golden Gate Bridge and the San Francisco skyline.However, the estate's size came with significant carrying costs. Agassi's family rarely used the property, and his financial advisers wanted him to sell it rather than continue paying to maintain a largely vacant home.The original asking price stood at $24.5 million. After several reductions, Agassi lowered it to $21 million about six months before the reported deal. Bullock explained why the couple became more flexible on price."When they considered the annual cost of that property to sit there vacant, they decided that they needed a little inducement for the marketplace and they started reducing the price,"The final $20 million offer still ranked among the Bay Area's most expensive home sales that year. Stuart Peterson, president of hedge fund Artis Capital Management, agreed to buy the estate. His fund had also been a major investor in YouTube before Google's $1.65 billion acquisition of the video-sharing company.Despite its impressive setting, the Tiburon property had a drawback. Built in 1976, the house had not received a major renovation since the mid-1990s. That left parts of the estate feeling dated to prospective buyers, making it harder to compete in the luxury market.Bullock said several wealthy visitors, including movie stars, had toured the home but ultimately passed on it. The buyer planned to make changes, although details were not disclosed before the transaction closed.Agassi had wanted the property for years. He first considered buying it in the mid-1990s while married to actress Brooke Shields, but she disliked the compound and discouraged the purchase. When it returned to the market, Agassi acted quickly rather than risk losing it again.By 2006, Agassi had retired from professional tennis and was living in Las Vegas with Graf and their two children. The couple were also exploring property development, including a luxury condo-hotel project in Idaho. Their Tiburon sale marked a shift away from a costly home they seldom used, even as they pursued new opportunities in real estate.
Article Summary: Andre Agassi and Steffi Graf agreed to sell the 3.5-acre estate for $20 million. The sale was expected to close in the first week of January 2007. The deal showed that even a high-end property in a sought-after location can struggle to find the right buyer.

Article Title: Travis Kelce’s $200 million investment in Six Flags draws attention as investigators examine Goliath’s safety record
Article Text:
​Travis Kelce (Getty Images)

Travis Kelce’s Six Flags investment meets renewed scrutiny

Six Flags Goliath investigation raises questions about ride safety

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Travis Kelce’s connection to Six Flags has taken on a different significance as a fatal roller coaster accident at Six Flags Over Georgia draws attention to ride safety. The Kansas City Chiefs tight end is an ambassador and investor in the amusement park company, making the developing investigation an important story for readers following his business interests beyond football. On October 12, 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after being ejected from the Goliath roller coaster. Four other riders, all minors, suffered non-life-threatening injuries. Authorities are still working to establish exactly what happened.Kelce has built a public profile that extends beyond his NFL career, with business interests and brand partnerships adding to his growing commercial presence. His role as a Six Flags ambassador and investor connects him to one of the best-known names in the amusement park industry.However, the fatal incident at the Georgia park raises serious questions about ride safety and operational oversight. It is important to distinguish Kelce’s business association from the investigation itself. There is no information in the available reporting that links the NFL star to the operation, maintenance or safety decisions involving Goliath.Six Flags Over Georgia reopened on October 16 for its Fright Fest event, but Goliath remains closed.Park officials have not announced a date for the roller coaster’s return, and the attraction cannot resume operation until state investigators complete the required review.The accident also places greater attention on how amusement parks maintain public confidence when a serious incident occurs. For a company with a broad entertainment business, safety assurances must rest on verified findings, transparent communication and effective oversight.Investigators are examining the circumstances surrounding Kariem’s death, including the ride’s operation and its restraint system. Cobb County police said preliminary witness and employee interviews indicated that Kariem was ejected, struck other riders and fell beneath the attraction.Several eyewitness accounts have raised further questions. Erica Billups told The Associated Press that her children encountered a restraint that repeatedly became unlocked about an hour before the fatal incident. Her account has not been independently verified by investigators, and officials have not established a connection between that reported problem and the death.State inspection records have also attracted attention. According to WSB-TV, records from Goliath’s March 16, 2026, inspection noted bushings that needed replacement. However, the state inspection reportedly recorded no violations, deficiencies, citations or red tags.The available records do not establish whether those components had any connection to the accident.Georgia authorities are reviewing evidence, interviewing witnesses and examining relevant records. The coaster’s manufacturer, Bolliger & Mabillard, is also investigating.For Kelce and Six Flags, the immediate issue is not speculation about responsibility but the need for a clear account of what happened. Until investigators establish the cause, questions about the restraint system, maintenance and ride procedures remain unanswered. The findings will be crucial to understanding the tragedy and determining what steps may be needed to prevent a similar incident.
Article Summary: Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce is an ambassador and investor in the amusement park company. On October 12, 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after being ejected from the Goliath roller coaster. Four other riders, all minors, suffered non-life-threatening injuries.

Article Title: Green Card ban: Tech firm Cloudera agrees to pay $2 million and accepts 2-year ban from PERM for discrimination
Article Text:
Cloudera agrees to pay $2 million to the DOJ and DOL for discriminating against US workers.

There are no exceptions: Harmeet K Dhillon

A California-based tech firm, Cloudera, has reached a settlement of $2 million with the Department of Justice and the Department of Labor on allegations that the company discriminated against qualified US workers when it filed for Green Cards for its foreign workers. Additionally, the company will be banned from the Green Card process for two years. Cloudera's Green Card ban was announced earlier -- before the Donald Trump administration banned the Green Card process of eight major tech companies, including Microsoft and Adobe. Cloudera's case is different as there was a lawsuit filed against Cloudera in April this year.“There are no exceptions: the Justice Department will hold accountable employers who discriminate against US workers,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “This substantial settlement, in partnership with DOL, sends a strong signal to employers that the federal government will work together to ensure employers treat US workers fairly.”In April, DOJ filed a lawsuit alleging that Cloudera alleging that the company violated the Immigration and Nationality Act by discriminating against US workers "when recruiting and hiring for seven positions under the PERM process".The Justice Department said that under the terms of the settlement,, Cloudera will establish a back-pay fund of $1.4 million to compensate qualified US workers who tried to apply for the jobs at issue but were not given fair consideration. Cloudera will also pay $600,000 in civil penalties to the United States."Cloudera will be subject to compliance obligations designed to ensure future adherence to federal labor and anti-discrimination laws. These measures include enhanced monitoring, revised PERM compliance procedures, and reporting requirements intended to prevent future violations," the department said.The PERM (Program Electronic Review Management) process is the mandatory first step for US employers sponsoring a foreign national for an employment-based green card (typically EB-2 or EB-3). It is designed to prove to the US Department of Labor (DOL) that there are no qualified, willing, and available US workers for the job, and that hiring the foreign worker will not lower local wages. But Cloudera asked applicants to send their applications an email address that did not accept outside emails.
Article Summary: California-based tech firm, Cloudera, has reached a settlement of $2 million with the Department of Justice and Department of Labor. The company discriminated against qualified US workers when it filed for Green Cards for its foreign workers. The DOJ filed a lawsuit alleging that the company violated the Immigration and Nationality Act by discriminating against US workers.

Article Title: After ditching Mamata Banerjee, Yusuf Pathan gets a gift from Gujarat government
Article Text:
The land has an estimated market value of Rs 20.53 crore, based on a valuation of Rs 2.10 lakh per sq m approved by the civic body.





VADODARA: The state govt has approved a proposal to allot a disputed 978 sqm Vadodara Municipal Corporation (VMC) plot in Tandalja area to former India cricketer and ex-TMC MP Yusuf Pathan , with 500 sqm to be gifted to him for residential use and the remaining 478 sq metres transferred at 55% of the assessed valuation.VMC municipal commissioner Arun Mahesh Babu confirmed that the civic body had received the govt’s approval for the allotment sought by Pathan. “However, the details are yet to be finalised, and the proposal will have to go through VMC’s standing committee and general board approval process,” he said.The proposal will be considered by the Standing Committee before being placed for General Board ratification.The decision comes nearly two months after Pathan and other rebel Trinamool Congress (TMC) Lok Sabha MPs broke away from Mamata Banerjee and announced their merger with Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) on June 14, 2026, following BJP’s victory in the West Bengal assembly elections. Pathan was appointed one of the national vice-presidents of NCPI.The proposal, prepared by VMC’s land estate department, concerns a plot in Tandalja under town planning scheme 22, final plot 90. The land has an estimated market value of Rs 20.53 crore, based on a valuation of Rs 2.10 lakh per sq m approved by the civic body.Govt’s resolution reached VMC at the end of Aug. Pathan later withdrew his appeal before Gujarat High Court against the rejection of his earlier claim to the plot.Under the resolution, 500 sq m of the municipal land will be allotted to Pathan as a gift for residential use. The remaining 478 sq metres will be transferred at 55% of the valuation determined by the valuation committee of Vadodara Urban Development Authority (VUDA) on March 17, 2026, amounting to a 45% concession against that valuation.The resolution states that the arrangement will not set a precedent for similar cases. It also provides that the revenue department will allot VMC land equivalent in value to the land transferred to Pathan.The controversy dates back to 2012, when Pathan sought a 99-year lease of the plot adjoining his family’s residence. In his application, he cited security concerns arising from his profile as an international cricketer and said the adjoining land would be convenient for residential use.The standing committee and general board approved the proposal to allot the plot directly to him without a public auction and forwarded it to the state govt for approval. In June 2014, however, the urban development department rejected the proposal, citing the need for a public auction or open bidding for valuable land.The civic body subsequently alleged that Pathan had fenced and occupied the plot despite the rejection. The issue resurfaced in June 2024, days after he won the 2024 Lok Sabha election, when VMC issued him a notice directing him to remove the alleged encroachment.Pathan challenged the action before the high court. His lawyers relied on a govt policy concerning allotment of land to international sportspersons, while VMC argued that the plot belonged to the civic body and could not be allotted without following the prescribed procedure.In Aug 2025, the high court upheld govt’s rejection. The court held that prolonged possession without an allotment order or payment did not create a legal right to the land.Pathan subsequently appealed against the order. During hearings in June 2026, a division bench questioned how he had taken possession of public land without completing the allotment formalities or making payment. The court also cautioned that continued occupation could increase his financial liability.On Aug 31, Pathan withdrew his appeal unconditionally.
Article Summary: The land has an estimated market value of Rs 20.53 crore, based on a valuation of Rs 2.10 lakh per sq m approved by the civic body. The controversy dates back to 2012, when Pathan sought a 99-year lease of the plot adjoining his family’s residence. In his application, he cited security concerns arising from his profile as an international cricketer.

Article Title: In 2020, an Ohio couple moved into a friend's home and spent $30,000 on its kitchen; six years later, an appeals court rejected their $215,000 purchase claim and revived the owners' eviction bid
Article Text:
The Claxtons said they renovated the house believing it would become theirs. (Representational AI image)

Friendship led to housing arrangement

The $30,000 kitchen renovation

How the failed purchase became an eviction dispute

Why appeals court rejected purchase claim

In 2020, an Ohio couple moved into a friend's home and spent $30,000 on its kitchen; six years later, an appeals court rejected their $215,000 purchase claim and revived the owners' eviction bidA couple in Ohio, who moved into a friend's house and spent $30,000 renovating its kitchen, have lost their claim to purchase the property for $215,000. Six years after they first moved in 2020, an appeals court ruled that the money spent on renovations did not give them a legal right to buy the house. The Wednesday decision also allowed the homeowners to pursue their eviction claim.The dispute involved Carl and Lane Claxton and their friends, James and Beverly Lupinetti, where an arrangement to help the Claxtons buy a house eventually turned into a disagreement over money, renovations, and ownership. According to court records , the Claxtons believed they had an agreement to purchase the property, while the Lupinettis maintained that the sale had never been completed.The matter reached court in April 2022, when James Lupinetti sought to evict the Claxtons from his Blue Meadow Lane property. The couple challenged the eviction and insisted that the house was supposed to be sold to them. In September 2025, a lower court ruled in their favour and ordered the homeowners to complete the $215,000 sale.However, the Ohio First District Court of Appeals overturned that decision. It found that the families had never entered into a binding agreement to sell the house.Although the Claxtons could no longer enforce the proposed purchase, the judges said they could still receive compensation for improvements made to the property.James Lupinetti and Carl Claxton had known each other for nearly a decade before the dispute began. They met while playing basketball at a YMCA around 2010 or 2011 and became friends.In 2019, James faced financial difficulties after his dump truck business failed. Carl, who had invested in the business, lent him $10,000. James agreed to repay $15,000, including interest.By 2020, James and Beverly had moved into a condominium, leaving their house on Blue Meadow Lane vacant. James was concerned about losing the property because he was struggling financially.At the time, mortgage payments on the house had been temporarily suspended under a Covid-19 relief programme. Carl expressed interest in buying the property, and the two families began discussing an arrangement.The Claxtons moved into the house in October 2020. They were allowed to live there without making housing payments until May 2021, when the mortgage relief period ended. James understood that this arrangement would also settle the earlier loan.After May 2021, the Claxtons began making payments directly to the mortgage lender while trying to arrange financing to purchase the house.While living in the property, the Claxtons began making changes to the house. They painted rooms, repaired damaged flooring and walls, worked on the septic system and renovated the kitchen. Both families later agreed in court that the kitchen renovation had cost $30,000.The Claxtons said they made the improvements because they believed the house would eventually belong to them. James, however, testified that he became concerned when he discovered the kitchen work in October 2021 because the couple had not yet purchased the property. He also told the court that he was willing to pay $30,000 for the improvements.Meanwhile, the proposed purchase was running into difficulties. The Claxtons obtained preliminary approval for a $215,000 mortgage, but a vehicle loan affected their ability to secure financing.They subsequently sold their Yukon truck in an attempt to resolve the problem. The families also signed documents in December 2021 outlining the proposed sale, but those documents specifically stated that they were not legally binding.Further attempts to arrange financing followed, including assistance from Carl's friend Ray Wilkins. However, the sale still did not go ahead. The parties gave different accounts of the financing problems and disagreements over the purchase price. On February 22, 2022, James informed Carl that he would no longer sell him the house.The collapse of the sale left the Claxtons living in a property they had hoped to own. In April 2022, James filed an eviction case, claiming that the couple owed $8,314.55 in unpaid rent.The Claxtons opposed the eviction. They argued that the homeowners had agreed to sell them the property and that the renovations supported their claim.The lower court initially accepted their position. In September 2025, it ordered the Lupinettis to sell the house for $215,000 and rejected the eviction claim. The homeowners appealed, bringing the dispute before the Ohio First District Court of Appeals.The judges found that the families had never signed a binding agreement to sell the house. Although the Claxtons had lived there, paid towards the mortgage and spent money on renovations, these actions were not enough to establish that the homeowners were legally required to sell it to them.The court also observed that the couple's mortgage payments were linked to their use of the property as a home and were not intended as payments towards buying it.As for the renovations, the judges found that spending money on improvements did not automatically establish ownership rights.The court also concluded that the Claxtons were tenants because they had agreed to pay the mortgage and utilities while occupying the house. Their failure to make the agreed payments for several months meant that the homeowners were entitled to pursue eviction.
Article Summary: Carl and Lane Claxton moved into a friend's house in 2020 and spent $30,000 on its kitchen. Six years later, an appeals court ruled that the money spent on renovations did not give them a legal right to buy the house. The Wednesday decision also allowed the homeowners to pursue their eviction claim.

Article Title: In 1968, Cassandra Henderson graduated from a North Carolina school; nearly 60 years later, she moved back into the same building after it was restored from 20 years of vacancy into 53 senior apartmen
Article Text:
Dillard School Senior ApartmentsPhoto credit: https://www.taxcreditcoalition.org/

A school with deep local meaning

From empty building to senior housing

Designed for ageing in place

Why adaptive reuse is important

A homecoming with a larger lesson

Cassandra Henderson graduated from Dillard Junior High in Yanceyville, North Carolina, in 1968. Nearly six decades later, she moved back into the same building, not as a student but as a resident of the newly restored Dillard School Senior Apartments. The former school, which had stood empty for about 20 years, has been transformed into 53 affordable apartments for seniors aged 62 and older, reported Tax Credit Coalition.The project is a rare example of a community turning a vacant historic building into practical housing. Originally built between 1949 and 1951, the Caswell County Training School was the first African American school in Caswell County to offer 11 grades. After desegregation in 1969, it was renamed for longtime principal Nicholas Longworth Dillard and continued serving students until it closed in 2002. Read more details about it here, as per Tax Credit Coalition's report:For generations of Black students in Caswell County, the school was more than a place to learn. It represented opportunity at a time when educational access was shaped by segregation. Its early name, Caswell County Training School, reflected the era’s segregated school system, but the institution became a centre of learning, pride and community life.The campus included a gymnasium addition in 1960, giving students space for athletics and gatherings beyond the classroom. Henderson’s graduation in 1968 came near the end of that era, just before desegregation changed the school’s role and identity.After desegregation, the school was renamed Dillard Junior High in honour of Nicholas Longworth Dillard, its longtime principal. The building continued to serve local students until its closure in 2002, after which it entered a long period of vacancy, as per the report.For two decades, the former school sat unused. Its future was uncertain until community-led preservation efforts helped secure its place on the National Register of Historic Places and build support for a new purpose.The restoration converted former classrooms into seven studio apartments and 46 one-bedroom apartments. All 53 units are restricted to seniors with incomes at or below 50 percent of the area median income, making the development an important affordable-housing option in rural Yanceyville. The project was developed through the work of DreamKey Partners and Red Stone Equity Partners. It also received recognition from the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition, which awarded Dillard School Senior Apartments its 2026 Recognition of Housing Tax Credit Excellence in the Rural Housing category.The apartments were designed to be more than simply affordable. The building includes elevator-served accessibility, a community centre with a business and computer room, fitness space, community laundry, tenant storage and on-site management with supportive service coordination, it was further reported.Outdoor amenities were also built into the plan. Residents have access to community gardens and recreation areas, including pickleball and shuffleboard courts, encouraging neighbours to stay active and connected.For Henderson, returning to the building meant rejoining a place filled with personal history. For other residents it provides a stable home in a familiar community with services and shared spaces designed for later life.The Dillard School project is an example of how historic preservation and affordable housing can go hand in hand. Rather than demolish a prominent local feature, the community preserved its structure and repurposed it to fulfilll a present-day need.Rural communities often struggle with a shortage of new homes, an ageing population and limited rental options. Turning an old school building into apartments for senior citizens can help address these problems while allowing older residents to remain close to familiar places and their communities.The project also demonstrates the value of patient, community-led redevelopment. The school’s revival did not happen quickly. It required years of vacancy, preservation advocacy, historic recognition and investment before it could become housing again.Cassandra Henderson’s return gives the Dillard School Senior Apartments a human story at their centre. A building that once shaped her education now provides her with a home, nearly 60 years after she walked its halls as a student.The transformation also offers a broader lesson for towns considering the future of vacant schools, factories and civic buildings. When communities protect historic places and adapt them carefully, they can retain memory while addressing urgent needs such as senior housing.Today, Dillard School Senior Apartments is a preserved landmark and active community. The 53 apartments are more than brick and classrooms returned; they are a new lease on life for a building that continues to serve the people of Yanceyville.
Article Summary: Dillard School in Yanceyville, North Carolina, was the first African American school in Caswell County to offer 11 grades. After desegregation in 1969, it was renamed for longtime principal Nicholas Longworth Dillard. The building continued to serve local students until its closure in 2002, after which it entered a long period of vacancy. The former school, which had stood empty for about 20 years, has been transformed into 53 affordable apartments.

Article Title: Sugar stocks tumble today: Bajaj Hindusthan, Renuka Sugars plunge up to 5%; here's why
Article Text:
Sugar stocks slip after govt's latest ethanol procurement tender

Oil firms drop sugar-based ethanol from 2026-27 tender

Grain-based ethanol takes centre stage

Sugar supply concerns behind the move

NEW DELHI: Sugar stocks turned sour on Monday, tumbling over 5% after the government halted sugar-based ethanol supplies for 2026-27.Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar led the losses among the listed companies, with its shares falling 5.22% to Rs 20.16 on the Bombay Stock Exchange in early trade. Dwarikesh Sugar Industries declined 4.45% to Rs 44.28, while Shree Renuka Sugars dropped 4.43% to Rs 21.16. Dalmia Bharat Sugar and Industries slipped 3.24% to Rs 466, Dhampur Sugar Mills fell 2.81% to Rs 191.90 and Balrampur Chini Mills lost 2.55% to Rs 704.35. EID Parry India was down 1.57% at Rs 683.75 on the BSE.The sell-off came after the latest ethanol procurement tender barred supplies made from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses. For sugar mills, the decision shuts the door on an important outlet for their produce, particularly one that offers higher margins.Dalal Street also started the week on a weak note, with the BSE Sensex slipping 307.63 points, or 0.41%, to 74,421.64, while the Nifty 50 fell 81.30 points, or 0.35%, to 23,096.80.The government has directed oil marketing companies (OMCs) to bring sugar diversion for ethanol production down to zero during the 2026-27 supply year.The restriction was set out in a tender issued by Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL) on October 16 on behalf of state-run OMCs. "The Government of India has issued directions that sugar diversion for ethanol be reduced to zero for ethanol supply year 2026-27," the tender document said, as cited by PTI.It further stated, "No offers have been sought for ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar or sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses in this quantity bid tender."The tender seeks bids for around 11 billion litres of ethanol for the period from November 2026 to October 2027. The volume is intended to meet the requirement of blending 20% ethanol with petrol under the nationwide programme.With sugar-based feedstocks excluded, the tender allows producers to offer ethanol made from maize, broken rice, surplus rice procured by the Food Corporation of India (FCI) and C-heavy molasses.However, the shift does not come with a higher incentive for maize-based ethanol. The procurement price has been reduced to Rs 68.86 per litre from Rs 71.86, while the incentive has been cut to Rs 2.79 per litre from Rs 5.79. The lower rates are expected to reduce returns for producers supplying ethanol made from maize.The changes reshape the feedstock options available to distilleries participating in the petrol-blending programme, which has so far drawn on both grain-based and sugarcane-based ethanol.The decision comes at a time when domestic sugar availability is under pressure from concerns over production. Poor rainfall in key sugar-producing states, including Maharashtra and Karnataka, has raised the risk of lower output, alongside concerns about rising prices.India, the world's largest sugar consumer, has expanded ethanol blending to reduce its reliance on imported crude oil. But the use of sugarcane and sugar for fuel also competes with the quantity available for domestic consumption, particularly when production is constrained.The latest tender seeks to balance these competing requirements: maintaining adequate sugar supplies and containing domestic prices while continuing the country's petrol-blending programme.India has adopted petrol containing up to 20% ethanol, known as E20, as the nationwide standard. Ethanol is produced from agricultural raw materials, including sugarcane and grains, and blended with petrol to replace part of fossil fuel consumption.The programme has opened up a substantial market for domestic distilleries and provided farmers with an additional source of demand for agricultural produce.For the 2026-27 supply cycle, however, the exclusion of sugar-based ethanol puts greater emphasis on alternative feedstocks. The availability of grain, procurement prices and distillery capacity will be important factors in meeting the programme's blending requirements.
Article Summary: Government halts sugar-based ethanol supplies for 2026-27. Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar leads the losses among the listed companies. BSE Sensex slips 307.63 points, or 0.41%, to 74,421.64.

Article Title: Bombay HC to hear on October 26 plea filed by actor Imran Khan against 'Leave India' order
Article Text:
The B​ombay High Court will hear the petition on October 26, as Imran Khan faces a departure deadline

Poll Vote & Share your view Should the government provide clearer criteria for issuing leave notices to foreign nationals? Absolutely, transparency is crucial. Not necessary, the system works as is. Maybe, but only if it changes often. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion





MUMBAI: Bombay high court on Monday said it will hear on October 26, actor Imran Khan Pal’s petition against a ‘leave India notice’ issued by the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer, (FRRO), Mumbai, to him on October 14, four days after a protest where he was detained. The notice requires him to leave the country, as a US national, by October 28.The HC asked the actor to also make State a party.Senior counsel Venkatesh Dhond for the actor mentioned the matter for urgent hearing. He said, “ this is a petition where a person who has been residing in India since he was 2 years old, is asked to leave without notice, without any hearing, without reasons…”.The actor has no criminal antecedents, Dhond said to a query. He said the petition mentions that he has no criminal record and no antecedents.The Chief Justice led bench before which the matter was mentioned asked if all parties were served a copy of the petition. Dhond said it was. The Additional Solicitor General Anil Singh for the Centre and FRRO, a central authority under the Bureau of Immigration said he received a copy of the petition “10 minutes ago.”Dhond sought a hearing the day after. Singh said it can be heard on October 26.Dhond said since the actor has been asked to leave by October 28 it would be cutting it too close. However, Singh said, “we will come prepared to argue the matter.”The actor, almost 44, had filed the petition on Saturday challenging the notice as “arbitrary, unreasoned and wholly misconceived’’ and against principles of natural justice.The notice flouts his fundamental rights to equality under Article 14 and to life under article 21 of the Indian constitution, his lawyers contended.On Saturday the actor also was issued a fresh notice this time a show cause notice on why his Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) status should not be cancelled by invoking a provision under the Citizenship Act that says for any action violatingArticles 14 and 21 are constitutional guarantees available to even foreigners in India, it underscored. He was given no reasons nor any reasonable opportunity to be heard and the notice was issued directly, the petition argued.The FRRO, had within four days of a protest in Mumbai against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, where the actor was present, invoked the Immigration and Foreigners Act (IFA) 2025 to issue him the departure notice on October 14. The notice is based on “purported contravention of uncited provisions of the IFA and the Rules and Orders’’ under it.His petition says , Merely …mechanically reproducing the words of a statutory provision is not sufficient in law and cannot be countenanced” It take a ground that the actor “who has lived in India for forty-two years, is apparently sought to be expelled solely because an FIR has been registered. The FIR is at the stage of investigation.The offences alleged under Sections 223, 126(2), 189(2), 189(3) and 189(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 are all bailable, and none carries a punishment exceeding two years. No charge-sheet has been filed, no court has taken cognizance, and no charge has been framed.Even if a charge-sheet were to befiled, the Court may decline to take cognizance. If it takes cognizance, the Petitioner may be discharged. If charges are framed, he may be acquitted.To expel the Petitioner at the very threshold of that process is to visit the ultimate consequence upon a mere allegation and to condemn him, in effect, on the mere recording by the police of an intimation of the commission of an offence.”The urgent interim relief the actor will argue for next Monday is a stay of the notice and final relief is to quash and set it aside.
Article Summary: Bombay high court will hear actor Imran Khan Pal’s petition against a ‘leave India notice’ issued by the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer, (FRRO), Mumbai, to him on October 14. The notice requires him to leave the country, as a US national, by October 28.

Article Title: 'Geography is real': Rubio says India-US trade deal close, explains Trump admin's stance on Russian oil
Article Text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio

Why the US is taking another look at Russian oil sanctions

Graham bill and geopolitics

NEW DELHI: US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Monday said that India and the US are close to finalising a trade deal. He also explained the reason behind Washington's consideration of India energy needs before imposing sanctions or tariffs linked to Russian oil.Speaking to reporters in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, Rubio said the US had waived some sanctions in recent months to limit their impact on global energy supplies and prices."We've had to waive sanctions over the past few months because of the impact on global supplies and prices...We have to manage all of these things.”Explaining how Washington was balancing trade negotiations with India and decisions on sanctions, Rubio said countries had to consider several factors when making foreign policy decisions, including how easily they could access alternative energy sources.“We're trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that. That's one of the things we taken into consideration when the President makes a decision about national security waivers and things of that nature. Every country has a complex set of factors that it has to take into account. Geography is real. For some countries, it's very difficult to acquire energy from alternative sources.That's not an excuse, but all of that has to be balanced when making foreign policy..."Rubio is currently in Uzbekistan and is scheduled to visit Mumbai on Tuesday to meet external affairs minister S Jaishankar. He will also travel to Jamnagar later in the week, which is home to one of the world's largest refineries.Rubio's remarks come after US President Donald Trump waived several sanctions related to Russian fuel sales that were due to take effect under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.The law, which has now been paused, would have allowed the US to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. India and China are among these countries.Rubio said the proposed measures would affect not just Russia but also countries that buy its energy. The US wants to use a 60-day period to study how the sanctions and tariffs could affect the global economy and its own economy."These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries—India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," Rubio said.He said India had diversified its energy sources but still bought a significant amount of energy from Russia. Switching to other suppliers immediately was not easy, he added."You've got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it's hard to pivot from one day to the next. But they're also an important ally and partner of the United States. So we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is," he added.Rubio also said the US was considering changes in the global situation since the Graham bill was passed. He pointed to the growing conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia, along with the war between Russia and Ukraine.He said global energy supplies were under pressure because of several factors, including Iran, the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and damage to energy infrastructure during the Russia-Ukraine war."I think when the bill was passed, one of the reasons the waivers were put in there is understanding that they would need some period of time to study this, given all the different things that are that are going on in the world right now, including the pressure on global energy supplies that are happening not just because of Iran and not just because of the Straits of Hormuz, but increasingly because of the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia, and because of the war with Ukraine and Russia, where energy infrastructure is being hit, and so that's having an impact on global prices as well," he said.Meanwhile, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal last week said that the first part of the agreement had been finalised and had moved to the legal drafting stage. "US bilateral trade agreement's first tranche has been finalised and it is going through final contours, the legal drafting and we hope to be able to finalise that soon and operationalise that once we get the competitive advantage over our peer countries," Goyal said.
Article Summary: US secretary of state Marco Rubio says India and the US are close to finalising a trade deal. He also explained the reason behind Washington's consideration of India energy needs before imposing sanctions or tariffs linked to Russian oil. Rubio is currently in Uzbekistan and is scheduled to visit Mumbai on Tuesday.
